Mr. Speaker before this Bill is read a second time, I desire to say a few words on a question which I think is of very much interest to the country at the present time. Going back to tihe year 1895, we were told by hon. gentlemen now on the treasury benches that they were the party of low tariff, that when they came into power the tariff would be reduced. The first action of the government in connection with the tariff was largely to increase very many items, notably coloured cotton goods of almost every character from the finished muslin to the coarsest cotton tweeds and ducks and denims worn by workingmen. Woollen goods were also increased. Women's shoes were increased from 25 to 30 per cent. Fur goods were increased from 25 to 30 per cent. I need not go on and enumerate the many articles on which the duty was materially increased preparatory to the application of the British preference, which was intended to bring the tariff down again t^a lower basis. However, the government "seems to have overlooked the fact that all the goods imported of the classes I have referred to on which the duty was increased were not brought in from Great Britain, but from 280
the United States and many other countries against which the higher tariff prevails, the result being that in many instances the duties were enhanced enormously, as I propose to show. I intend to refer only to a few articles, because time would not permit this morning that I should deal at any length with the question. I will take the case of watches, an article which every gentleman and every lady desires to have, and therefore an article of common consumption. Under the old tariff the duty on watches was 25 per cent; under the new tariff the duty is 27* per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From what countries?
The schedule is 271 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But there are three schedules.
I am speaking of the general tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But my hon. friend is not fair when he ignores the British preference.

I am going to show the result even when you apply the British preference. I am going to be perfectly fair, because I want the people to understand [something more of the nature of the tariff that we have at the present time. Taking all the watches that came in from other countries and including those that came in under the operation of British preference, the average rate of duty paid in 1909, the last year for which we have full returns, instead of being 25 per cent as under the old tariff was increased to 29-90 per cent. All the watches we imported under the British preference was $1,641 worth, whereas we imported under the general tariff $10,559 worth from Switzerland and $16,157 worth from the United States. So that the people paid the larger tariff, the general tariff, on the larger quantity of imports. Taking a common article like brushes, used in every household, we find that the old Conservative national policy duty that was so much complained of was 25 per cent, whereas under the present tariff the general rate is 271 per cent. The average rate paid in 1909 was 27-4 per cent, an increase of 2-4 per cent over the duty under the national policy. Shawls were imported under the old tariff at 25 per cent, whereas under the new tariff, under the general schedule, the duty is 35 per cent; the average paid in 1909 was 33-.64 per cent instead of 25 per cent under the much-abused National Policy. Ribbons, 30 per cent under the old tariff] 35 per cent under the new tariff, making an average of 35-20. I shall have something to say of this item a little lateT. Ladies' blouses and shirt waists, an article of

.8843

*every-day use worn by the ladies, were 32i per cent under the old tariff, that is the general rate; under the new tariff 35 per cent, the average rate of duty paid in 1909 being 33 per cent or one-half per cent more than under the old and much abused National Policy tariff. Take lead pencils, a small thing it may seem, yet an article that is in use in every household, an article that is extensively used in the province of Ontario by every child _ going to school, and yet even the little children are taxed higher than before; 25 per cent was the duty under the old tariff, 27i per cent is the duty under the new tariff, that is the general duty, but taking into consideration all the various duties, British preference, general tariff, intermediate tariff, and surtax, the average rate of duty paid in 1909 was 29-22 per cent -or nearly 41 per cent higher than under the much abused National Policy tariff. Bailway rugs were 25 per cent under the old duty and were raised to 35 per cent, making an average in 1909 of 30-12 per cent. Then we have fishing rods. The sportsmen had to pay 30 per cent under the old tariff and 30 per cent under the new. That is a case different from the others where the duty was reduced to 26 per cent. Clocks were 25 per cent under the old tariff and 30 per cent under the new, I mean the general tariff, the average being 31 -14 per cent. Corsets, were 324 under the old tariff and are 35 per cent under the new, making 34-31 as the average rate of duty in 1909 instead of 321 paid prior to the advent of the present low tariff government. Ready-made clothing under the old tariff was 5 cents per pound and 30 per cent, equivalent in 1896 to 341 per cent. The present government raised the general duty to 35 per cent. Of course, the British preference has been applied, but notwithstanding that the duty in 1909 averaged 33-77 per cent. Baths, batting and sheet wadding was 221 per cent under the old tariff and under the new tariff was increased to 25 per cent, making an average duty of 25-2 per cent as against 221 under the old tariff. Then we come to the items of guns and firearms. These were 20 per cent under the old tariff, and were raised to 30 per cent. Then the British preference was applied and the deduction of one-third brought it back again to 20 per cent. However, as I stated before, the government omitted to take into consideration the fact that we do not import all the guns from Great Britain. We import largely from the United States, so that the average rate of 'duty paid on guns was 271 per cent instead of 20 per cent as under the old tariff, and yet hon. gentlemen will tell us that they have reduced the tariff. Now, I have given these concrete examples, selected examples of various kinds of woollen goods; I have spoken of cotton goods and
other articles of manufacture, so that the people may have their attention dra-wn to the fact that this government that promised a reduction in tariff has actually given us large increases. Now, we may demonstrate that in some other way, but before proceeding to give other statistics, I propose to give one or two illustrations of how the new tariff works. Take the article of lead pencils to which I referred a moment ago. There were imported last year, I mean in 1909, from Great Britain $11,091 worth. These came in under the British preference and got the benefit of the one-third off, and had we imported pencils from no other country than Great Britain certainly the duty would have been reduced. But we imported from the United States $117,303 worth as against $11,081 worth from Great Britain. Now, the result of that is that whilst under the old tariff the duty paid would have been $50,852, the new duty in 1909 was $59,446, making an increase on this little item alone of $8,594. And yet these gentlemen go through the country and boast that they are the low tariff party. Take the article of ribbons, which I think is a very good illustration of the effect of the tariff. This is an article used in every house. The ladies, the children, little girls, all like to be decked out in ribbons. The government seem to know this, and they say: if you will beautify yourselves by wearing ribbons, we will make you pay for them, and here is the way it works out. We imported from Great Britain in 1909, $13,584 worth of ribbons. We imported from France $320,553 worth. These came in under the general tariff of 30 per cent instead of 25 per cent. From the United States we imported $92,386 under the general or higher tariff. From Switzerland we imported $361,394 worth, all under the general tariff, whilst we imported from Great Britain under the British preference or reduced tariff only $13,584 worth. Altogether under the general tariff we imported $1,288,609 worth, whilst, as I stated before, under the British preference, all we imported from Great Britain was $13,584 worth. Now what is the effect when we compare this duty with what it would have been under the old tariff? The duty on ribbons under the old tariff would have been $402,616. On the $1,342,054 worth which we imported under the present tariff we paid a duty of $472,671, or in all, we paid $70,055 more duty on ribbons alone in 1909 than we would have paid had the old duty remained in force. And ,yet hon. gentlemen sav they are the party of the low tariff.
On one single article of every^ day wear, every day purchase, the actual increase in duty is $70,055. I would think statements like this ought to be startling to the country, and to open the eyes of the people to

the fact that this government have not redeemed their pledges to give a reduced tariff. I would not complain so much if they had not increased it, but the duty has been increased, and that is what I complain of. I complain that the duties to-day are abnormally high as compared with what they were under the previous government. On certain articles they are reduced no doubt, but there are others on which they are largely increased and unfortunately the articles on which the tariff ought to be maintained are those on which the duties have been reduced. Had the government applied this increase of duty to support Canadian industries, there would have been a justification for it, but when you apply it to articles that are produced in this country or are produced to only a
very limited extent, and compel the people to pay high taxation without giving the benefits of employment of labour in the country or of protection, I say that the people do not agree with that kind of tariff. We are told that taxation has been reduced. Time and again this has been said, and last session the Minister of Customs particularly boasted of it. I shall give a table which I think will conclusively demonstrate that taxation, on the whole, instead of being reduced has been increased. The Minister of Finance gave us an important table giving the population of the country from 1891 down to the year 1910. I propose to utilize that table to show how taxation has been increased. That table is as follows:	'
Year.	Customs Duties.	Excise duties.	Total Taxation.	Rate per Capita.1896....	S19,S33,229 46,064,598 61,031,336	$ 7,926,006 14,010,220 15,108,633	$27,759,285 60,074,818 76,139,969	) $ 5 461906	9 601910 	10 21
Thus, the average per head of taxation for the year ending March 31, 1910, is $10.21 as against $9.60 in the fiscal year 1906, and as against $5.46 in the Last year of Conservative rule, 1896.
I shall take another plan to show how taxation has been increased. Hon. gentlemen in making their comparisons in the increase of taxation put together the amount of dutiable, and the amount of free goods. The dutiable goods are the only goods with which we have to deal in the matter of taxation, for, as we all understand, free goods pay nothing. It may be argued that a number of articles have been put on the free list, and that that ought to be taken into consideration. I grant it. Corn, for example, has been put on the free list, but when corn was put on the free list the government, being anxious not to lose the revenue, largely increased the duty on sugar, making up the loss they had sustained by putting corn on the free list. In 1909 the duty on raw sugar was $2,673,423. Under the old rate of half a cent per pound the duty in 1909 would have been $2,267,125, an increase under the present tariff on the imports of raw sugar for 1909 of $406,298. That is the people of this country pay as duty on sugar $406,298 more than they would have paid had the tariff of the Conservative party remained in force. I remember that a year ago the Minister of Customs drew attention to the fact that this duty was on raw sugar. He said the people of this
country did not consume raw sugar, that they were so well off that they consumed refined sugar. The Minister of Customs need not have made that statement, because it is well known that refined sugar is the article that goes .into consumption in this country. He should have told us at the same time that the refined sugar is made from the raw, that the raw sugar is simply the basis from which the refined sugar is obtained, and the moment you increase the duty on the raw sugar you increase the duty on the refined sugar. I wish to make a comparison on the importation of corn. The importation of com in 1909 amounted to $5,414,672. This came in free. Out of this we exported 303,321 bushels leaving 5,111,351 bushels as comsumed in Canada. The old duty on this amount of corn consumed in 1909 would have been, at the rate of 7i cents per bushel, $383,351. Nowr, we take the added duty on raw sugar of $406,298, and deduct the loss on the com of $383,351, and we find as between those two articles that the government takes out of the pockets of the people $22,947 more than they would have done had they left com at the old rate of 7J cents a bushel, and left sugar at the old rate of i cent a pound. What advantage is it to the people of the prairie provinces that corn should be put on the free list? They are not purchasers of corn. I do not understand that com is imported from the United States into the great west, and consequently they get no advantage whatever

from the reduction of the duty on corn. But they are every one of them taxed heavily for the increased duty on sugar which they have to pay while they get no advantage from the reduced duty on corn. I submit that problem to hon. gentlemen from the west, and ask them if they have received fair treatment in the matter of these two items of com and sugar.
There is one other consideration I desire to submit. As I said before, I am going to deal with the dutiable goods only, because it is rather a matter of no importance to many people who consume dutiable goods whether some other person gets an article free of duty. For example, what advantage is it to the lady who goes down Sparks street and buys a muslin dress, or any other dress, on which the duty has been increased; what advantage is it to that lady whether manufacturers of agricultural implements get their iron and steel free of duty, or at a reduced rate of duty? She gets no advantage out of the reduction of duty on iron and steel, hut she is compelled to pay the high duty on all she purchases herself. Better would it be if these duties were so regulated that all parties would pay their fair share, and that the duty would not be taken off, or almost entirely taken off, to the benefit of only one class of the community, while another class is compelled to contribute to the revenue of the country. I say, therefore. we have only to deal with dutiable goods in order to ascertain what the taxation of the country is. In 1896, dutiable goods imported into this country amounted to $74,259,940, on which a duty of $20,290,037 was paid, making an average rate of duty that year on dutiable goods of 27-22 per cent. Now, I will come down to the year 1897, when there was a slight reduction. The amount of dutiable goods imported into the country was $74,108,590, paying a duty of $19,891,996, giving an average rate of duty of 26-84 per cent for that year, a slight reduction of the taxation of 1896. _ A revision of the tariff took place again in 1897, when the government seemed to need more revenue. In 1909, two years after the last tariff came into force, we imported in dutiable goods alone, $185,329,094; on these there was paid a duty of $52,670,287, making an average rate of taxation in 1909 of 28-28 per cent, as against 27-22 per cent in the last year of Conservative rule; and yet hon. gentlemen will tell us they have reduced the taxation.
Are these calculations made only upon goods which pay duties? Do they take any notice of goods put on the free list? I am asking for information.
I am only dealing with the dutiable goods, as I told the House.
The hon. gentleman would _ surely give the government credit for being- reducers of the tariff in respect to the articles on which they abolished the duty altogether.

I have done so. I gave the government credit for reducing the duty on corn, putting it on the free list, and for increasing the duty on raw sugar at the same time; but the increase on raw sugar was more than the reduction on corn. Now, it so chances that the constituents of my hon. friend in Alberta do not buy corn; consequently, putting corn on the free list was of no advantage whatever to the people of Alberta.
Corn is not the only article.
I am giving that as an illustration, and I might give many others. But every man in the province of Alberta buys sugar, the hon. gentleman knows that.
They do not all use it, a large number.

I think there are very few who do not use it. I think if I were in the hon. gentleman's place, I would have hesitated to make that statement. Sugar is an article of household use, and the people who consume sugar pay the increased duty, and if they do not consume corn they get no advantage in respect to corn. As I said, the lady who goes down Sparks street and buys a dress which is subject to a heavy duty, gets no advantage whatever out of the reduction of duty given to the manufacturers of mowers and reapers on their iron and .steel. Con-, sequently, I am justified in dealing with dutiable goods, and those alone. Now, some people may question the propriety of my saying that the taxation in 1909 was $52,670,287. I desire to make plain what those figures mean. The actual customs duty paid that year was $48,059,791. But apart from that, there was an increased duty on tobacco paid as an excise duty; nevertheless it was taxation, and we must add that in order to determine what the taxation of the country was. There was also paid in that year as bounties, $2,467,308. Who will venture to say that that is not taxation? I may be told by the Finance Minister that this was paid out of revenue. So it is. The Postmaster General has a surplus, a large surplus, and a large amount of these bounties may be paid out of that surplus. There is revenue also from other sources; the public works of my hon. friend produce a revenue, and it may be out of this revenue that the bounties are paid. They may be paid out of various sources of revenue, and possibly not a dollar of these bounties is paid out of customs revenue; perhaps the larger

part is paid out of excise revenue. So I am not counting the item twice, I am perfectly fair, it is something added to the taxation. No man can question the fact that the payment of bounties is just another system of protection. It reduces the duties on iron and steel to give the manufacturers of iron and steel a bounty instead of the duty that was imposed. Practically it is a duty, to all intents and purposes. Therefore, I am perfectly justified in saying that the duty in 1909 was $52,670,287, making an average rate of 28-38 per cent, or about 1 -16 higher than the average rate of duty on dutiable goods in the last year of Conservative rule.
Now I contend that there is a feeling abroad all over the country, and I sympathize with it, that there ought to be a hewing down of these extreme duties, more especially on articles which are not made in the country, but which people have to buy, and which are imported from other countries, and which constitute practically a direct taxation. I submit this proposition as a fair criticism of the government's tariff policy, and I have no doubt when they come to reduce their tariff they will take matters of this kind into consideration. Just fancy, on that one article of ribbons alone to-day the people of this country pay over $70,000 more in duty than they would have paid had the tariff of 1896 had remained in force. Examples such as I have given will tend to open the eyes of the people to the fact that they are being subjected to a system of high taxation that I do not think the circumstances warrant.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much regret that my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) did not do us all the honour of presenting this criticism of the tariff at an earlier stage of the session when we might have had an opportunity of doing him the courtesy of examining it in detail. Much of it, however, is a mere reproduction of the hallucinations which my hon. friend has permitted himself to entertain for a number of years and which, I suppose, he means to carry down to the end. Some features of his criticism, however, are somewhat new.^ We have reached a stage of the public business when I am sure we shall all desire condensation, and if I reply very briefly to him he will be aware that I have no desire to be discourteous to him, but that it is simply because time is precious. As to the general statement that there has been no reduction in the tariff I can only say that it is almost an amusing statement to me whenever I hear it made. We have discussed time and time again this question and I have presented to the House in detail lists of hundreds of items on which tariff has been reduced. They are
all to be found in 'Hansard/ fully set forth and I shall not waste the time of the House by attempting to go into them. My hon. friend may select here and there some particular case. He says that there were some cases in which the tariff was increased but he forgets that if the general tariff was increased with regard to some items it was substantially reduced as respects the British preference, with a proper desire of turning trade towards Great Britain rather than towards foreign countries. Where _ goods coming under our tariff are not chiefly^ produced in Great Britain it is quite possible that in the cases of those particular articles the tariff works in the way of an increase. But take the standard staple articles, such as my hon. friend has mentioned, and what do we find? He says that the duties on cottons are higher than they were in former years and he makes the extraordinary statement that the duties on woollens are higher. The duties on woollen goods under the old tariff ran from 40 up to 50, 60 and 70 per cent. The duties on woollen goods under our present tariff were reduced. As every one knows^ woollen goods are articles which are, in a peculiar manner, the product of Great Britain, and if you have the duties reduced under the British preference, what folly it is to talk about these duties being increased under the general tariff which applies to countries which do not send us goods of the same class. Great Britain is the greatest competitor in woollen goods. Germany is a competitor to some extent, but Germany has not such favourable rates of duty. The duties on woollen goods have, if I may use the expression, been enormously reduced. Perhaps I should qualify that and say that they have been largely reduced-reduced so much, that from the other side of the House time and time again, the complaint has been made that we have reduced these woollen duties. But after all, we have to deal with the tariff as a whole and not with any particular individual item. My hon. friend asks what value is it to the lady who goes down to buy her ribbons if she has to pay a higher price? What concern is it of hers that the duty on agricultural implements is reduced? If the lady could deck herself out in ribbons only and be received in respectable society my hon. friend's criticism might be useful, but if that lady decked herself out in ribbons only-
You would not have her deck herself out in mowing machines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but it is the mowing machine of the husband that enables her to buy ribbons.
Suppose she had no husband

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then she had better get one, and in this country she will get one very quickly. In the happy days prevailing now, any good woman cam readily get a good husband. There might be some excuse for her not having a husband in the olden times when every man could not support a wife, but in these happier days which now prevail she can get a husband readily and he can support her well and afford to buy her ribbons and silk dresses. Then my hon. friend enunciates the most extraordinary doctrine with regard to duties on dutiable goods only. My hon. friend says that all you have to consider is the duties on dutiable goods. What folly! Suppose we should put 90 per cent of our importations on tire free list and. to the remainder add 5 per cent in duties, what would be the result? True, the duties would be increased on one-tenth of our imports, but- on nine-tenths of them we would pay no duty at all, and then my hon. friend would say that it would make no difference what we did in regard to the free list, that it is only the dutiable list that we have to do with. Then he points out that the duty on ribbons has been increased. If you make 90 per cent of the imports free and only tak.e the dutiable list it might be easy to show that there has been'an increase on particular articles. But, the payment of duties must be determined in the aggregate. We have discussed that matter over and over again in the House. It has been shown that, taking the imports into Canada of goods which have been brought from other countries, if the old tariff had remained in operation the people of Canada would have paid tens of millions of dollars more in duties during the last fourteen years than they have paid. It is not necessary to take up the time of the House by going^ into that matter in detail, hut that fact will be apparent to any person who looks at the figures. Another argument that my hon. friend has brought in here is that bounties mean an increase of taxation in addition to. Could anything be more ridiculous ? I was surprised to find my respected friend bringing that old yarn in here again. I would have thought that he had got over that delusion. He says we do not know where these bounties come from, whether they are taken out of the post office revenue, customs revenue or excise. He does not and we do not. Nobody can tell what particular source of revenue pays any particular item of expenditure. The revenue all goes into the common pot and it is paid out of the common pot for the benefit of the public services of 'the country. There is no difference between the fund out of which you pay a bounty and the fund from which you take the indemnity of a Mr. HENDERSON.
member of this House. They both come from the same source.
Are they charged to the same account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is another question. We are not now discussing the question of charges against income and capital.
My hon. friend does not charge them to the same account. He eliminates them from the same account in order to show a surplus.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is another question, which I will be happy to discuss with my hon. friend when I have more time. I intend now to confine myself to the points made by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) and to only a few of them because I have not the time to deal with them in detail. There is no means of determining what particular source of revenue pays the bounty. The revenue all goes into the common treasury, and the charges upon that revenue come out of the common treasury. A merchant may go into a customs house and pay $10,000 in duties and it goes into the revenue account. Next day one of the steel companies comes along and makes application for $10,000 in bounty and the money goes out. My hon. friend says that makes $20,000 of taxation. The $10,000 collected from the merchant went into the revenue and next day it went out to pay the bounty. There is $10,000 of taxation, but my hon. friend calls it $20,000 and he puts that in as a part of his statement. Surely my hon. friend must see that the thing is too ridiculous to admit of a monent's legitimate discussion.
Where do you put it?
That is a kindergarten argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then if it is I am addressing kindergarten pupils. It is the old story of the amount of taxation that a man pays. My hon. friend, in his delusion, takes the amount of revenue. collected, and the various sources of taxation, and makes1 up what he calls a statement of taxation.
' I am not going to inquire whether the figures are correct or not; I am going to assume that they are correct. It is not a question of the amount of taxation that a man pays, but it is a question of the burden that it levies upon him. If in former times he could afford only one suit of clothes at a certain season of the year, he bought but one suit of clothes, and paid perhaps $5 into the customs on it. In these more prosperous times he will buy perhaps two suits of clothes and pay $10 in customs. He pays more taxation, but is he not better off? The rate of taxation is lower than it was before, but by reason of the

greater prosperity, by the better times that have come to him, he can. buy more goods, and instead of regretting that kind of increased taxation, I am glad that the prosperity of the people is so great that they are buying more goods, even although they thereby pay more taxes.
My hon. friend talks about there being no reductions. The curious thing is that whenever he comes to individual items, when we are dealing practically with these matters, he is generally commenting on our reductions.

The minister misquotes me if he says I contended there were no reductions. I could not have been more plain than I was. What about the corn? Did I not say it was made free, and that there were reductions under the British preference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but my hon. friend insists on misleading the House, as well as himself. I know he does not do so intentionally, but he deceives himself. The hon. gentleman lays down the most marvellous doctrines of political economy. He says that when you increase the duty on raw sugar you thereby increase the duty on refined. Could anything be more preposterous? You increase the duty on raw sugar, but the duty on refined is fixed in the tariff, you increase it or not as to amend the tariff in respect to it.
I think the minister will find I spoke of the price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then let us take it at that. The price of sugar in Canada is not governed by the duty on raw sugar. The price of the raw sugar affects the profits of the manufacturer, but the people, as my hon. friend says, do not eat raw sugar, but refined, and the price of refined sugar in Canada is largely governed by the tariff on refined sugar. My hon. friend says we have increased the duty on refined sugar.
On the raw sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He does not eat any raw sugar. What difference for our argument whether the manufacturer is making more or less money; the difference between the raw and refined affects the manufacturers profits. As a matter of fact when this government came into power the duty on refined sugar was $1.14 per 100 pounds, and t'he duty on British refined sugar-and it is only from Great Britain it comes practically-is 72 cents per 100 pounds. Yet my hon. friend goes out and tells the people that we have increased the duty on the sugar the people eat.
Ceriainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The people do not use the raw sugar; the difference is that the
refiner has less protection than before, hut I believe that owing to the greater consumption and the increased business of the country he has been able to do very well. Whenever we do make a reduction my hon. friend is found to complain. In the little schedule we have had before us yesterday he regretted the decrease in the duty on leather.
You allowed the Americans to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Never mind how it is done, my hon. friend is complaining about there being no reductions and yet when we make reductions he complains. We reduced the duty on lime, but when we make the reductions,-and the hon. gentleman only mentioned these two items of leather and lime-he regretted that we had made them. How are wre to satisfy my hon. friend? When we reduce the duties he will not be pleased, and when we increase them he is displeased.

My complaint in regard to lime was that it was not properly classified. I claim that there is no reduction in this article if we classify it right. In the other article, of leather, two years ago you increased the duty and suddenly, after men had put their capital in the businessi, without notice, you decreased the duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to their being no notice, tariffs are introduced for increase or reduction without notice; that is one of the advantages of our system that no one knows in advance of any changes. This 'arrangement with the United States does not affect the classification of anything. My hon. friend's complaint is that we are reducing the duty on this according to our custom classification and yet the whole trend of his speech to-day is that we are to make no reduction at all. There are many other points in my hon. friend's speech that I would gladly take up, but I feel that I should not detain the House.

The Act to amend the law respecting the Aid of Dry-docks will, it is believed, lead to the early construction of docks capable of receiving the largest warships and thus assist the movement for naval defence.
The Act making provision for the lease of lines connecting with the Intercolonial railway, and for their operation as a part of the system of government railways, will enlarge the sphere of usefulness of the Intercolonial, and tend to increase the development and prosperity of an important section of the Dominion.
The appointment of a commission to incxuire into the needs and present equipment of the Dominion as respects industrial training and technical education should prove an important contribution to the work of the provinces in advancing the industrial development of Canada and the welfare of its working classes.
The measure to revise and amend the Insurance Act, which engaged the attention of parliament in the previous session, has now been completed and is likely to prove an effective and satisfactory law.
The amendments made to the Currency Act, with special reference to the production of a Canadian gold coinage at the Ottawa branch of the Royal Mint, marks another step in the advance of Canada.
The arrangement lately made between the United States and Canada, averting a threatened tariff conflict and opening the way for negotiations which give promise of further improvement in the commercial relations of the two countries, has, I am glad to know,
given much satisfaction to the people on both sides of the boundary line.
Equally gratifying is the termination of the long standing tariff dispute with Germany upon terms which fully recognize the important principle for which Canada contended, and which encourages the expectation of an extended and mutually beneficial trade, between the German empire and the Dominion.
The Act for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers, will, it is hoped, without injuriously interfering with commercial and industrial enterprises, effectively protect the public against attempts to restrain trade unduly.
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
I thank you for the liberal provision you have made for the public service.

My official connection with Canada is drawing to a close. My interest in it, however, will not be severed. I shall continue to watch its progress and development, with the sincere hope and belief that under God's providence it will ever increasingly prosper.
